articleTitle: Development of an Equivalent Fault Model for the Grid-Interlinking Converter of DC Microgrids to Predict Fault Resilience
abstract: Increasing penetration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) in distribution systems is changing the fault behavior in these systems due to different characteristics of IBRs compared with conventional generators. This paper proposes an equivalent fault model for the grid-interlinking converter (GIC) of DC microgrids to evaluate their fault resilience against grid-side faults. Developed based on the detailed linear dynamic model of the GIC, the proposed model will enable the prediction of transient and steady-state fault behavior of the GIC under grid symmetrical faults with higher computational efficiency suitable for large-scale simulations compared with electromagnetic transient (EMT) models. The proposed equivalent fault model, which is based on dependent current sources, is tested under symmetrical faults with various fault resistance values under both rectifying and inverting modes of operation of the GIC. Simulation results verify the small prediction error of the proposed model for both transient and steady-state fault values.

articleTitle: Understanding Line Losses and Transformer Losses in Rural Isolated Distribution Systems
abstract: Rural, isolated power systems in the mainland United States and in states like Alaska and Hawaii are powered by assets like diesel generators. These rural, isolated power systems cannot operate at the higher band of medium voltage (like 69 kV). They primarily operate in the 12–14 kV range to keep the cost of the distribution investments lower. Because of this mid-band medium-voltage range, the diesel consumption from line losses and distribution transformer losses is significant (almost 10% of the peak load). This work considers one such isolated power system and presents key findings about online losses and transformer losses. Understanding and documenting the impacts from losses is critical for communities that operate these power systems so they can take actions to reduce expensive diesel consumption. In this paper, we will present one such typical grid and model it in the electromagnetic transients domain. We used the tower structure and underground cabling installation to develop high-fidelity models of the lines. We also used high-fidelity models of distribution transformers to present the no-load losses and full-load losses. We present technical solutions that are available commercially off-the-shelf to reduce losses and reduce diesel consumption. This work will be a primer for communities to understand the technical challenges and possible solutions for rural, isolated power system operators.

articleTitle: Application of Fault Indicators for Substations and Feeders with Distributed Energy Resources
abstract: This paper summarizes the proper implementation of Fault Current Indicators (FCI) at substations and feeders with distributed energy resources. This includes the principal of operation, installation, options, and obstacles faced when selecting and designing FCI placement. Additionally, this paper discusses the benefits to operations and maintenance (O&M) teams by reducing outage times depending on the selected options such as local versus SCADA integration. A summary is provided to highlight the complexities and benefits.

articleTitle: Case Studies in WYE & Delta Distribution Capacitor Installations
abstract: Distribution engineers are familiar with the many benefits of shunt capacitors in providing VARs to magnetize the iron in induction motors and other Inductive devices. The benefits may include the reduction of line and transformer copper losses, and improvement in voltages at the load. However, improper installation and operation of both delta connected capacitors and wye capacitors can reduce their effectiveness and contribute to premature capacitor call failures. This paper addresses three (3) case studies of capacitor installations where capacitor operations were compromised. Suggestions are included in the paper to improve the understanding of capacitor operations. This should provide safer and more efficient capacitor operation.

Author Keywords: power factor correction reducing system losses

articleTitle: Developing More Accurate Load Flow Studies for Extreme Winter Peaks
abstract: Load flow studies are essential for planning and operating electric power systems. However, the accuracy of these studies can be affected by a number of factors, including the ambient conductor temperature. During extreme winter peaks, the ambient conductor temperature can drop significantly below 25°C, the default value used in many load flow software programs. This can lead to inaccurate results, particularly regarding voltage drop. This paper presents a case study investigating the accuracy of load flow studies during extreme winter peaks modeling various ambient conductor temperatures. The case study uses real-time meter demand and voltage data to compare actual recorded meter voltages to WindMil calculated voltages. The results of the case study show that using an ambient conductor temperature of 25°C during extreme winter peaks can lead to the model-calculated voltage drop being higher than the actual. However, using a lower ambient conductor temperature can significantly improve the accuracy of the load flow results thus potentially reducing the necessary capital expenditure from recommended system improvement projects.

articleTitle: Implementing a Pole Fire Mitigation Strategy Case Study
abstract: Pole Fires represent an increasing threat to electric utility operations reliability, and public safety. There is a substantial risk resulting from collateral damage both to public property and participation in wildfire ignitions. This paper introduces the causes of pole fires and mitigation strategies. Conditions that lead to pole fires are reviewed, as well as the risk to line workers and first responders. Finally, a case study demonstrating the opportunity to mitigate pole-fires through strategic initiatives is discussed.

articleTitle: The Challenges of Modeling Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) as Blackstart Resources and for Volt-VAR Optimality
abstract: Modeling, testing and instituting Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) as Blackstart Resoucrces presents several challenges due to the fundamental differences between traditional black start resources (e.g., large generators) versus DERs like solar PV systems with battery storage. This paper addresses some of these key challenges. These include intermittency of coordinating DERs to provide continuous power during a black start event, especially during extended periods of cloud cover or when battery energy storage is depleted. This paper additionally addresses the collapsing voltage and stability control challenges specific to maintaining bulk power system stability during black start synchronization These physical and engineering limitations require careful engineering design, modeling and engineering to ensure that DERs can support critical loads and substations during black start events. A variety of additional challenges also exist. Additionally, there are challenges associated with feeder location and low voltage secondary system impacts on DER functions and settings. We compare typical functions and settings for DERs for power factor control and correction. We also demonstrate how voltag control via Volta-VAR power factor correction can be done

articleTitle: Analysis of Autotransformer Modeling Techniques in Power System Studies
abstract: An autotransformer is a transformer that has its windings coupled both magnetically and electrically. An auto-transformer can be configured using a standard two-winding transformer by connecting one of the windings in series with the other. In this configuration, both the source side and the load side share one winding, which is called the common winding. The other winding, which is connected in series to the common winding, is called the series winding. Autotransformers are smaller, cheaper, and a good alternative to a two-winding transformer if the desired voltage transformation is small. A general rule of thumb is that the voltage transformation should be no greater than a factor of three. There are two primary applications for autotransformers in distribution systems: voltage regulators and step banks. Voltage regulators have adjustable tap settings and can adjust voltage by ±10%. Step banks are parts of a distribution system where the voltage change is moderate. A common voltage transformation for a step bank is by a factor of two, for example, 24.94Y-12.47Y kV. While there is extensive literature that provides adequate models for autotransformers in voltage regulation applications, there is significantly less literature on the modeling of autotrans-formers for step bank applications. In this paper, four different models of autotransformers used for step bank applications are analyzed and compared. The first method of modeling is to use a standard grounded-wye-grounded-wye two-winding transformer with impedance values and a power rating that reflect an autotransformer. The second is the same standard grounded-wye-grounded-wye two-winding but with a corner-grounded delta tertiary. The third is a true grounded-wye-grounded-wye autotransformer. The last model is a true grounded-wye-grounded-wye autotransformer with a corner-grounded delta tertiary. These models are all used in a small four-node test feeder to analyze their performance under balanced steady-state operation, unbalanced steady-state operation, and balanced and unbalanced fault conditions. In addition, a detailed description of the variations among these models is emphasized.

articleTitle: Grid Services Co-Optimization of Battery Energy Storage Systems with Conservation Voltage Reduction
abstract: Peak demand management is implemented in a number of ways including the dispatch of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and the utilization of Conservation Voltage Re-duction (CVR). This work studied and tested the co-optimization of the operation of both technologies and considers the addition of a BESS inverter operating off of unity power factor (PF) utilizing one of North Carolina Electric Cooperatives' (NCEC) microgrids (MGs). NCEC owns and operates multiple Distributed Energy Resources (DERs), including MGs, and desires to expand their operational capabilities to include grid services. First a study modeled CVR, BESS dispatch, and off unity BESS operation for peak demand management. Findings from the study were then incorporated into field tests to validate dispatch strategies and conclusions from the study. Real and reactive power injection during a CVR event was found to be the optimal dispatch strategy for the microgrid BESS that was studied. This optimal dispatch strategy was effectively implemented during the testing that was conducted.

articleTitle: Development And Application Approach of EV Impact And Mitigation Analysis Methods for Use In Traditional Rural Electric Utility Planning Practices
abstract: To reduce greenhouse emissions and pollution, the U.S. is witnessing a rapid growth of electric vehicle (EV) adoption. The increasing EV charging demand will be additional load to electric utility distribution systems, which may cause undervoltage and thermal overloading on circuits and transformers. Studying the potential impact of EV charging on distribution grid and coming up with methods and strategies to manage and overcome the challenges is critical to maintain the system reliability and available service capacity. This paper presents the results of a recent project on studying the impacts of potential EV growth on West Kentucky Rural Electric Cooperative Corporation, a rural electric distribution cooperative, circuits using different EV charging profiles using EPRI's DRIVE and OpenDSS tools. IEEE Standard C57.91-2011 and C57.110-2018 are utilized to study the thermal dynamics of transformers due to EV charging considering harmonics. This paper also studies the potential impact of newly DOE-proposed efficient transformer based on amorphous metal core on transformer temperature rise. An approach to integrate the analysis methods with daily, traditional utility distribution planning process using Milsoft's Windmil commercially available software to mitigate transformer temperature rise due to EV charging is also discussed. A method of using real time monitoring of transformer temperature for thermal model validation and optimal EV charging is proposed. This paper also presents an ambient-temperature-adjusted transformer rating method, and the technical aspects and economic benefits to utility retail residential rates brought about by the methods.

articleTitle: Practical Application of IEC 61850 in U.S Substations Compared to Traditional Relay Protection
abstract: IEC61850 is a part of the International Electrotechnical Commission's (IEC) Technical Committee 57 (TC57) architecture for electric power systems. This paper highlights some practical applications of the improved technical capabilities, available under IEC 61850, over typical and legacy substation relay protection design. Improved digitalization of the substation can be leveraged into improved operational efficiencies and reduced construction time & material. This paper identifies some common applications and value-adding opportunities including better electrical protection, reduced wiring requirements, and improved expansion flexibility of a substation. In addition, specific use cases are highlighted where applying the standard is a practical option, such as “load shedding” and “breaker failure” schemes. The paper also includes general comparisons of design efficiency gains and reductions in capital costs and construction time.

articleTitle: Identifying High Value Microgrid Deployment Options Across Four Military Distribution Systems with the MicrogridUP Methodology
abstract: Distribution systems hosting multiple critical loads with stringent resilience requirements such as military installations could benefit from microgrid deployments to cost-effectively meet continuity of operations and resilience requirements. However, existing electric grid planning tools lack integrated methods for concurrently modeling on-site generation with low voltage (building), medium voltage (distribution system primary), and high voltage (transmission systems) interconnection. This short-coming in existing planning tools increases time, cost, complexity, and uncertainty in designing microgrids for multi-building sites. The MicrogridUP project has created a comprehensive microgrid planning framework to address known software and planning problems that limit the widespread, cost-effective utilization of coordinated microgrid deployments, especially on military sites. The project team includes utilities that hold utility privatization (UP) contracts to own and operate electrical infrastructure on behalf of the military. The framework has been used to develop microgrid plans for four mililtary installations these utilities serve. National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) Research's MicrogridUP planning framework has been able to identify attractive microgrid candidates, optimize their placement and components, and reduce the soft costs associated with the planning process. In this paper, we present an overview of our multi-staged optimization approach to microgrid planning and present microgrid opportunities that have been identified at 4 military installations served by 3 cooperative UP owners.
